title: Increase me in knowledge
hook: say, my Lord, increase me in knowledge (20:114)

segments.voice: Yesterday, your mother's eyes: Musa returned to the riverbank mother. Your line was so she would not grieve. Did a mother get some comfort from you? Day four hundred seventy-eight.

A student in the front row writes so fast to catch every word that half of what's said slips past. The pen is ahead of the understanding. The commentators, drawing on a hadith, describe something like it in the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: when the angel Jibril brought a passage, he would repeat each word as it came, hurrying, afraid of losing a single one. Ta-Ha has a verse for that moment. It tells him not to hurry, and then it gives him words to ask with.

Verse one hundred fourteen begins with praise: exalted is God, the true King. Then: don't hurry with the Qur'an before its revelation to you is complete. Another surah, Al-Qiyamah, says the same thing more vividly: don't move your tongue to rush it; We will gather it and recite it for you. In other words, the knowledge is safe; you can breathe. And then, in Pickthall's words: "and say: My Lord! Increase me in knowledge." In Arabic: rabbi zidni 'ilma. Some commentators point out something about this verse: they count it as the one place in the Qur'an where the Prophet is told to ask for more of something. Not more wealth, not more time, not more followers. More knowledge. And the word 'ilm in the Qur'an is wide. It's knowledge of God first, but it isn't only that. It includes understanding, discernment, knowing how things work and how to live. Tradition says the first word revealed to him was iqra': read, recite. Here, years later, the request is: more. A hadith in Ibn Majah and Tirmidhi preserves a prayer of his that builds on the verse: he asked God to make what he'd learned useful, to teach him what would be useful, and to increase him in knowledge. That's the balance of the verse: don't rush what's coming, and keep asking for more. Some Muslim students say rabbi zidni 'ilma before they study, before an exam, before opening a book. Six words in English. Three in Arabic.
screen: `DON'T HURRY IT.` · `ASK FOR MORE KNOWLEDGE.` · `'ILM: KNOWING, UNDERSTANDING.` · `USEFUL KNOWLEDGE, AND MORE.` · then, large: `MY LORD! INCREASE ME IN KNOWLEDGE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of something you don't know but would like to: a word in another language, how your car's engine works, the name of the tree outside your window, the meaning of a verse you've heard all your life. Choose one. Picture yourself learning it today, without rushing, the way the verse asks. If you pray, you can say rabbi zidni 'ilma, my Lord, increase me in knowledge. The bell holds the time.
'Ilm. Knowledge, wide in the Qur'an: the Prophet was told in Ta-Ha to ask his Lord for more of it. Today's word.
Your line: rabbi zidni 'ilma. Today, learn the one new thing you chose, and take your time understanding it. Day four hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims say rabbi zidni 'ilma, from 20:114, before studying, teaching or exams, and it can be seen written up in classrooms in Muslim communities.
